newsitem.title: UK: Markets prefer "big bang" switch into euro - ISMA.
newsitem.headline: Markets prefer "big bang" switch into euro - ISMA.

text.p: Securities firms would have preferred a "big bang" switchover to the euro instead of its more gradual introduction, an ISMA study said on Thursday.
Many firms expected the gains for the market post-EMU would be considerable and outweigh potential losses, said the study, commissioned by ISMA and involving 900 members across Europe.
International Securities Market Association (ISMA) is the international bond market's main self-regulatory organisation.
The extra costs of maintaining a parallel currency system between 1999 to 2002 was of considerable concern to market participants for reporting purposes, the study said.

The third stage of European economic and monetary union (EMU) is due to start in 1999, when the euro will be introduced alongside existing European currencies. EMU-participating currencies would be phased out by 2002.
The study said benefits could come from the following:
* There would be opportunities for credit trading within the debt market.
* There would be more room for diversification in so-called "exotic" currencies.

* The emergence of the euro should be viewed as a form of "market deregulation" as it removed market barriers. It said many believed that after the initial consolidation phase, massive growth in the longer term would follow.
But there were also a number of concerns, the report said.
* The disappearance of intra-European forward foreign exchange and intra-European currency swaps with the introduction of the euro.

* Currency support business within the euro-zone would have to shrink. Foreign exchange sales of European currencies to the fund management community would contract substantially. Some of the larger financial institutions active in the area of currency sales have reported they would retain only one out of every six of their currency sales team, the report said.

* A large number of opportunities in intra-European bond trading and arbitrage would inevitably disappear. Continental European banks foresaw, on average, a drop of 50 percent or more in their intra-European bond trading and arbitrage business.
* Uncertainty surrounded the re-denomination of the existing stock of government bonds.
